title: Hearing the Unspoken: Simulator-Induced Asymmetric-View Policy Optimization for Proactive Task-Oriented Dialogue
claim: Conditioning on hidden user states shifts agents far beyond what sampling or standard RL achieve, which only nudge behavior.
layout: 1 scatter plot, bottom-left to top-right, long arrows vs short arrows
description: A single scatter plot. The x-axis is the proactivity score from an LLM judge (1–5), and the y-axis is acceptance rate (%). Two model sizes are shown, Qwen3-8B in green and Qwen3-4B in blue. Each starts from a filled Vanilla dot at the lower left. Short thin arrows lead to Pass@16 (open circles) and GRPO (pink diamonds). Thick dashed arrows with a cream glow run up and to the right to gold stars, which mark the version with latent concerns. The left side is labeled 'Reactive plateau' and the right side 'Latent-concern regime', with a faint background gradient from cool to warm. Callouts read '+30.3 pp' and '+32.2 pp'. A legend at the bottom right explains the markers and the small-shift and large-unlock arrows. The eye goes first to the stars at the top right.
caption: Pilot study. Latent concerns move agents from the reactive plateau to the high-proactivity/high-acceptance regime, whereas sampling and GRPO provide only small shifts.
abstract: Proactive task-oriented dialogue (TOD), such as outbound sales, requires an agent that proactively elicits and addresses the user's concerns within a bounded number of turns, supports an informed voluntary decision, and respects refusal. Yet post-trained LLMs are inherently conservative, and reward-shaping RL (e.g., GRPO) struggles since it only re-weights what an already passive policy samples. We show that, in our evaluated settings, conditioning on the user's latent concerns induces proactive behaviors that the tested sampling budget and outcome-only RL do not reliably induce, establishing these concerns as a substantially stronger training-time signal. To operationalize this finding, we build the Cognitive User Simulator, which models each user as a stratified persona comprising observable external traits and hidden internal concerns. The simulator produces faithful and diverse interactions, while emitting per-turn state dynamics that track persuasion progress. We then introduce Simulator-Induced Asymmetric-View Policy Optimization, which converts the modeled concerns and the simulation state transition into complementary training objectives: (1) Asymmetric On-Policy Self-Distillation that transfers concern-aware behavior from a privileged view of the same policy into its deployable, conversation-only view; and (2) State-Transition Policy Refinement where the final decision provides trajectory-level advantage while synchronous state transitions refine turn-level credit direction. Across two real-world-inspired food-delivery settings (merchant and courier outbound recruitment), our method outperforms strong RL baselines (on Qwen3-8B, concern solving/acceptance rates rise from SEAD's 40.4/36.3% to 52.6/48.5% on merchant and from 36.7/33.5% to 45.6/44.3% on courier), is competitive with the evaluated proprietary LLMs under our evaluation protocol, and generalizes across the tested unseen LLM-based user simulators.
